quote.text: It is not the oath that makes us believe the man, but the man the oath.
quote.author: Aeschylus, fragment (5th c. BCE)

stories.headline: A Ship Burns Where the Deal Was Supposed to Be
stories.dek: A bulker was abandoned in flames off Oman on the night of 3–4 August, one seafarer missing, hours after Trump gave Tehran a "last chance before decapitation" and Rubio claimed progress. Iran, again, denied it is talking to Washington at all — only to Oman, only about the strait. Oil, which had fallen on the deal talk, bounced on the fire.

stories.kicker: The Macro Desk · The Portfolio Lens
stories.headline: A Record High, Bought on an Unsigned Deal
stories.dek: Oil fell almost 5%, equities printed records, and a global all-world portfolio sat within a whisker of its all-time high — all of it resting on a Hormuz agreement that, as The World notes on p3, no one has actually signed.

stories.headline: The Cathedral on the Assembly Line
stories.dek: This summer, the hottest thing to do in China on a weekend is to go and watch a factory work. It is a Xiaohongshu check-in craze, a policy campaign, and — read closely — a mirror the West is not ready to look into: the same building that means loss in Detroit means the future in Shenzhen.

stories.headline: The Defendant Who Didn't Show
stories.dek: Lim Tean was due at the State Courts at noon on 3 August to begin a jail term. He did not arrive, his lawyer could not reach him, and a warrant of arrest was issued for a sitting opposition leader — with a review of that warrant now fixed for 17 August.

stories.headline: One Bid for the Waterfront
stories.dek: The first residential plot in the Greater Southern Waterfront closed on 4 August with exactly one offer — yet that lone bid came in above what the valuers had guessed. A strong price and a thin field, arriving together, is the tell the whole market is now reading.

stories.headline: China Pulls Its Own Silicon Forward
stories.dek: Huawei has moved its next accelerator, the Ascend 950DT, into service months early, with DeepSeek's next model lined up to run on it. The pitch is compute independence. The catch is that the fabs behind it still can't make enough — and the price of everyone's silicon is rising in step.

stories.headline: The Flagship That Lets You Change the Battery
stories.dek: Sennheiser's MOMENTUM 5 Wireless has been out since June; what's new is the verdict. The review wave has settled on a sound-first over-ear whose real trick is quiet heresy in a sealed-in category — a battery the owner can replace.

stories.headline: A Ryokan Trades Its Kaiseki for a Wine List
stories.dek: Hoshino Resorts reopened KAI Matsumoto this week after a full renovation — and did something its brand has never done: replaced the traditional kaiseki dinner with a refined Italian menu paired to Nagano's own wines. It is either a clever read of the modern traveller or a small heresy, depending on who you ask.

stories.headline: Weezer Promises Its Angriest Record
stories.dek: Three decades and twenty albums in, Weezer calls the self-titled "Gold Album," out 21 August, "the most violent Weezer album ever." It is a claim, not a review — and the calendar is thick with claims this month, from a sooner DMA's LP to two late-August tentpoles no one has scored yet.

stories.kicker: The Family Desk · Screens & the Law
stories.headline: The Ban They Signed, the Rule They Live
stories.dek: Australia wrote the world's toughest law against under-16s on social media. Eight months in, its own regulator finds more than eight in ten of them still scrolling. The lesson for a Singapore household is less about the wall than about the door nobody guarded.

stories.headline: The Community That Negotiates Everything
stories.dek: In a week when the powerful keep announcing agreements no one has signed, this desk descends into the one subculture built the other way round — where nothing proceeds without an explicit, negotiated yes. Strip away the mythology and consensual kink behaves less like a fetish than like a craft: obsessive about gear, organised around workshops, and governed by a discipline it calls consent.

stories.headline: Two Hours of Iron a Week — and Not Much More
stories.dek: A thirty-year study of nearly 150,000 adults finds a strength-training sweet spot around 90 to 120 minutes a week, with the benefit flattening — and in places reversing — past it. For a mid-40s optimiser, the useful news is the ceiling, not the floor.

stories.headline: What's Worth Booking
stories.dek: A thick autumn is filling up — a stadium run of pop, a sumo basho whose good seats vanish the day they go on sale, and the digital-art room the eleven-year-old will actually thank you for.
